Stop all experiments and wait for AI technology to become more mature over several years
Focus on fewer use cases with clear owners, success metrics, and a path to production

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Concentrating on fewer, well-owned use cases with production plans converts experiments into value.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Launch even more experiments so that at…: More experiments without focus repeats the problem.
• Let the data science team choose projects…: Technique-driven choices often lack business ownership.
• Stop all experiments and wait for AI…: Waiting forgoes learning and value.

Key takeaway: Focus on fewer, owned use cases with a path to production.

stem: A bank's AI strategy must balance innovation with regulatory obligations. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Let each business line choose AI use cases independently without any central risk coordination
Avoid all AI use until regulators publish detailed rules for every possible banking use case
Launch customer-facing credit decisions first, since they have the highest value and fastest payback
Pursue use cases in tiers, starting with lower-risk internal uses while building governance for higher-risk ones

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tiered adoption builds capability and governance on lower-risk uses while preparing controls for regulated, higher-risk uses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Let each business line choose AI use cases…: Uncoordinated adoption creates inconsistent risk handling.
• Avoid all AI use until regulators publish…: Waiting for complete rules stalls progress.
• Launch customer-facing credit decisions…: High-risk uses first magnify regulatory exposure.

Key takeaway: Sequence AI adoption by risk while building governance.

stem: A company wants to track whether its AI investments are paying off across the portfolio. Which practice helps most?

choices.text: A count of AI initiatives launched each year, since more initiatives indicate better returns overall
A regular portfolio review comparing each initiative's measured results with its business case
A survey asking employees whether they feel the company is doing enough with AI tools
A yearly total of AI spending without linking it to any specific initiative or outcome

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Comparing actual results with planned value for each initiative shows which investments pay off and where to adjust.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A count of AI initiatives launched each…: Initiative counts are activity.
• A survey asking employees whether they feel…: Sentiment is not return on investment.
• A yearly total of AI spending without…: Spending alone says nothing about return.

Key takeaway: Review AI investments against their business cases regularly.

stem: An AI tool reduced manual data entry, but the finance team struggles to quantify the value because the saved time is spread across many people in small amounts. Which approach gives a defensible estimate?

choices.text: Measure time per task before and after on a sample, then multiply by task volume and loaded labor cost
Report no value at all, since small time savings spread across people can never be measured
Assume every employee saved one full day per week and multiply by the company's total headcount
Use the vendor's marketing estimate for average savings, since it applies equally to all companies and industries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sampling task times before and after, scaled by volume and cost, produces a transparent estimate grounded in the company's own data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Report no value at all, since small time…: Distributed savings can be measured by sampling.
• Assume every employee saved one full day per…: An arbitrary assumption is not defensible.
• Use the vendor's marketing estimate for…: Vendor averages are not company-specific.

Key takeaway: Estimate distributed time savings by sampling task times and scaling by volume.

stem: Which is an example of a leading indicator, rather than a lagging indicator, for an AI sales assistant?

choices.text: Year-over-year change in average customer lifetime value for the past two years
Annual revenue growth reported at the end of the company's fiscal year
The share of sales reps using the assistant weekly for proposal drafting
Final win rate reported at the close of the company's fiscal year

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Adoption on target tasks appears early and predicts later outcomes, while revenue and win rates are lagging results.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Year-over-year change in average customer…: Lifetime value changes are lagging.
• Annual revenue growth reported at the end of…: Annual revenue is lagging.
• Final win rate reported at the close of the…: Final win rate is lagging.

Key takeaway: Track leading indicators such as adoption to anticipate outcomes.

stem: A company must decide whether to build an AI capability that is central to its customer promise. Which reasoning supports building it in-house?

choices.text: Vendors never allow customization, so buying is never possible for important capabilities
Building in-house is always cheaper than buying, regardless of the capability's complexity
In-house builds are faster in every case, since internal teams never have any competing priorities to manage
Owning a core differentiating capability allows control over quality, data, and pace of improvement

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For capabilities central to differentiation, owning them provides control and a lasting advantage, even if building costs more.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Vendors never allow customization, so buying…: Many vendors offer customization.
• Building in-house is always cheaper than…: Building is often more expensive.
• In-house builds are faster in every case,…: In-house builds are not always faster.

Key takeaway: Build what is core to your differentiation.

stem: Two companies use the same foundation model for underwriting. One keeps improving its results each quarter. Which practice most likely explains this?

choices.text: Changing the assistant's name every quarter to keep employees excited about using the tool
A feedback loop that captures outcomes and expert corrections to improve prompts, data, and models over time
Using the model in more AWS Regions than the other company, which improves the model's quality
Paying for a premium support plan with the model provider that includes weekly vendor meetings

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Continuous improvement from real outcomes and expert feedback compounds, creating an advantage competitors using the same model do not have.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Changing the assistant's name every quarter…: Renaming does not improve results.
• Using the model in more AWS Regions than the…: Region count does not affect quality.
• Paying for a premium support plan with the…: Support plans do not improve underwriting quality by themselves.

Key takeaway: Feedback loops turn a common model into a compounding advantage.

stem: A company wants to decide which department should pilot its first generative AI tool. Which criterion matters most?

choices.text: A department with a clear, measurable pain point and a leader willing to own the pilot
The department whose office is closest to the IT team, for convenient in-person support
The department that has used the fewest software tools historically, to maximize novelty
The department with the most employees, since larger teams always produce better pilots

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pilots succeed with a clear problem to solve, measurable outcomes, and an engaged owner who drives adoption.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The department whose office is closest to…: Office proximity is minor.
• The department that has used the fewest…: Novelty is not a success factor.
• The department with the most employees,…: Size does not guarantee success.

Key takeaway: Pilot where there is a clear pain point and a committed owner.

stem: An AI project has high expected value but also a 30% chance of failing to deliver. A second project has lower value with a 5% failure chance. How should they be compared?

choices.text: Choose whichever project the most senior executive personally prefers without further analysis
Always choose the lower-risk project, since any meaningful risk of failure is unacceptable
Compare risk-adjusted value, considering both expected benefit and probability of success
Always choose the higher-value project, since risk should not influence investment decisions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Risk-adjusted comparisons weigh benefits by their likelihood, giving a fairer basis for choosing between options.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Choose whichever project the most senior…: Preference is not analysis.
• Always choose the lower-risk project, since…: Some risk is acceptable for sufficient reward.
• Always choose the higher-value project,…: Ignoring risk can destroy value.

Key takeaway: Compare AI investments on risk-adjusted value.

stem: Which statement best describes a platform approach to AI compared with a point-solution approach?

choices.text: A platform solves exactly one problem, while point solutions provide shared capabilities for many teams
Point solutions are always more strategic than platforms, regardless of the company's scale
A platform is always a physical hardware device installed in the company's own data center
A platform provides shared capabilities many use cases reuse; point solutions address one need each

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Platforms enable reuse across use cases, reducing marginal cost and time for each new one; point solutions are faster for single needs but duplicate effort at scale.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A platform solves exactly one problem, while…: The definitions are swapped.
• Point solutions are always more strategic…: Neither is always more strategic.
• A platform is always a physical hardware…: Platforms are not necessarily hardware.

Key takeaway: Platforms enable reuse; point solutions solve single needs.

stem: A company's AI strategy was written two years ago. Which TWO developments most justify revisiting it now? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Significant changes in AI capabilities and costs that open new opportunities
A new employee joined the strategy team and prefers a different writing style
The strategy document's formatting no longer matches the new brand template
The original strategy's author has moved to a different office building
Changes in the company's business priorities or competitive landscape

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Strategy should evolve when technology shifts or business priorities and competition change.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A new employee joined the strategy team and…: Writing style is not a strategic reason.
• The strategy document's formatting no longer…: Formatting does not affect strategy.
• The original strategy's author has moved to…: Office moves are irrelevant.

Key takeaway: Revisit AI strategy when technology or business context changes.

stem: Which TWO costs are most often underestimated in AI business cases? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The cost of naming the AI initiative and designing its internal logo
The cost of printing the business case document for the quarterly board meeting
Change management and training for the people who will use the system
The cost of the kickoff meeting's catering for the project team
Ongoing monitoring, maintenance, and model updates after launch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Post-launch operations and people-related change costs are commonly missed, which inflates projected returns.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The cost of naming the AI initiative and…: Naming costs are trivial.
• The cost of printing the business case…: Printing costs are trivial.
• The cost of the kickoff meeting's catering…: Catering costs are trivial.

Key takeaway: Include operations and change-management costs in AI business cases.

stem: A company can buy an AI solution that meets 80% of its needs today or build one that meets 100% in 12 months. The need is urgent but not a core differentiator. Which choice fits best?

choices.text: Do nothing until a vendor offers a solution that meets every requirement completely
Buy the 80% solution now and adapt processes or extend it where needed
Buy the solution and also build the custom one in parallel for the same need
Build the 100% solution, since meeting every requirement is always worth any delay

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For urgent, non-core needs, a good-enough solution now usually delivers more value than a perfect one later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Do nothing until a vendor offers a solution…: Waiting for perfection forgoes value.
• Buy the solution and also build the custom…: Doing both wastes resources.
• Build the 100% solution, since meeting every…: Delay has real costs for urgent needs.

Key takeaway: For urgent, non-core needs, prefer good-enough solutions now.

stem: A company's executives want AI to reduce costs, while its product team wants AI to create new revenue. How should the AI strategy handle this?

choices.text: Avoid choosing, and let each team pursue its own goals without any shared priorities
Pick only cost reduction, since revenue growth from AI is never achievable in practice
Balance the portfolio with both types of initiatives tied to explicit priorities and targets
Pick only revenue growth, since cost reduction from AI never produces measurable financial results

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A strategy can include both efficiency and growth initiatives, with explicit priorities and targets that reflect the company's goals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Avoid choosing, and let each team pursue its…: Lack of shared priorities fragments effort.
• Pick only cost reduction, since revenue…: AI can create revenue.
• Pick only revenue growth, since cost…: AI can reduce costs measurably.

Key takeaway: Balance efficiency and growth initiatives under shared priorities.

stem: A company uses AI to personalize its website and sees a conversion lift. Which step best confirms the lift is real?

choices.text: Run a controlled experiment where some visitors see personalization and others do not
Compare this month's conversions with a month two years ago before personalization began
Assume the lift is real because the vendor reported similar results for other customers
Ask the marketing team whether they believe the personalization has increased sales

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A randomized experiment isolates the effect of personalization from other changes and seasonality.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Compare this month's conversions with a…: Old comparisons include many other changes.
• Assume the lift is real because the vendor…: Other customers' results do not confirm this lift.
• Ask the marketing team whether they believe…: Beliefs are not measurements.

Key takeaway: Confirm AI impact with controlled experiments.

stem: A company's AI assistant is used by employees with visual impairments. Which responsible AI consideration applies most directly?

choices.text: Making the assistant available only on desktop computers in the main company office building
Making the assistant use only images in responses so that answers are more visually engaging
Making the assistant's responses as long as possible so that every user receives full detail
Making the assistant accessible, for example compatible with screen readers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inclusive design means the tool works for people with different abilities, such as through screen-reader compatibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Making the assistant available only on…: Restricting devices reduces access.
• Making the assistant use only images in…: Image-only answers exclude visually impaired users.
• Making the assistant's responses as long as…: Length does not address accessibility.

Key takeaway: Design AI tools to be accessible to all users.

stem: A company learns its AI hiring screen rejected qualified candidates from one university more often. Which response best reflects responsible AI practice?

choices.text: Delete the logs showing the pattern so that the issue cannot be raised by candidates later
Investigate the cause, correct the system, and review affected decisions where possible
Announce that the university's graduates are less qualified, based on the model's decisions
Keep using the system unchanged, since the company did not intend to treat anyone unfairly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Responsible practice means finding and fixing the cause of unfair outcomes and addressing harm to those affected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete the logs showing the pattern so that…: Destroying evidence is unethical and may be unlawful.
• Announce that the university's graduates are…: Treating a biased output as truth compounds the harm.
• Keep using the system unchanged, since the…: Intent does not remove harm.

Key takeaway: When AI harms people, investigate, correct, and remediate.

stem: A process owner says a new AI claims workflow will be 'human-in-the-loop.' What does this mean for how the process runs?

choices.text: A person writes every output by hand while the AI system watches and records the work
A person answers customer calls while the AI system listens for training data collection
A person reviews or approves AI outputs at defined points before action is taken
A person physically operates the computer hardware that runs the AI model at all times

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Human-in-the-loop places people at decision points to review, approve, or override AI outputs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A person writes every output by hand while…: That removes the AI's role.
• A person answers customer calls while the AI…: Listening for training data is not oversight.
• A person physically operates the computer…: Operating hardware is not oversight.

Key takeaway: Human-in-the-loop = people review or approve at key decision points.

stem: A company must decide who approves a new customer-facing AI use case. Which approach reflects good governance?

choices.text: The engineer who builds the system approves it alone, since they understand it better than anyone else in the company
A defined approval path that includes business, legal, security, and risk perspectives based on risk tier
Any employee can approve it, since AI use cases should never be slowed down by governance
The vendor approves it, since the vendor built the underlying foundation model being used

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clear approval paths with relevant perspectives, scaled to risk, ensure balanced decisions and accountability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The engineer who builds the system approves…: Builders approving their own work lacks independence.
• Any employee can approve it, since AI use…: No approval process means no governance.
• The vendor approves it, since the vendor…: Vendors are not accountable for the company's use.

Key takeaway: Define risk-based approval paths with multiple perspectives.

stem: A company's AI model uses customer data collected for billing to predict churn. What governance question arises first?

choices.text: Whether the churn model's dashboard will be ready for the next quarterly business review meeting
Whether the model should be retrained daily or weekly to keep the predictions current
Whether the billing team would like to receive a copy of the churn predictions each month
Whether using the data for this new purpose is permitted under consent and privacy obligations

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reusing data for a new purpose may require checking consent, notices, and legal basis under privacy rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Whether the churn model's dashboard will be…: Dashboard timing is operational.
• Whether the model should be retrained daily…: Retraining cadence is technical.
• Whether the billing team would like to…: Sharing results is secondary.

Key takeaway: Check purpose limitation before reusing data for AI.

stem: Which role is most important to name for each production AI system?

choices.text: An accountable business owner responsible for its outcomes and ongoing oversight
A travel coordinator responsible for booking trips for the model's developers
A designer responsible for choosing the colors and fonts of the system's user interface
A facilities manager responsible for the office where the model's team sits

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Each AI system needs an accountable owner who answers for its outcomes and ensures it is monitored and reviewed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A travel coordinator responsible for booking…: Travel is unrelated.
• A designer responsible for choosing the…: Interface design is not accountability.
• A facilities manager responsible for the…: Facilities are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Every production AI system needs an accountable owner.

stem: A company's AI assistant might give outdated policy answers after policies change. Which control reduces this risk?

choices.text: Increase the assistant's temperature so that answers vary and users double-check them
Train employees to ignore the assistant whenever a policy question seems important
Add a footnote telling users that policies may have changed since the assistant was trained
Keep the assistant's source documents current and re-index them whenever policies change

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Keeping sources current and refreshing the index ensures answers reflect the latest policies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increase the assistant's temperature so that…: More randomness increases errors.
• Train employees to ignore the assistant…: Ignoring the tool defeats its purpose.
• Add a footnote telling users that policies…: A footnote does not correct wrong answers.

Key takeaway: Keep AI knowledge sources current.

stem: A company deploys AI to draft responses to regulator inquiries. Which safeguard is essential?

choices.text: Automatic sending of drafts to regulators to reduce the company's response time
Expert review and approval of every draft before it is sent to the regulator
Using the most creative model settings so responses sound more persuasive
Deleting drafts after sending so there is no record of AI involvement

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Regulatory communications carry legal and reputational risk; expert review ensures accuracy and accountability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic sending of drafts to regulators to…: Unreviewed sending risks errors with serious consequences.
• Using the most creative model settings so…: Creativity is inappropriate here.
• Deleting drafts after sending so there is no…: Removing records undermines accountability.

Key takeaway: High-stakes AI outputs need expert review before release.

stem: Which risk is most associated with AI systems trained on data scraped from the internet?

choices.text: Running more slowly than systems trained only on internal company data
Being unable to answer any question written in a language other than English
Inheriting inaccurate, biased, or copyrighted content from the source data
Requiring more electricity to display results on employees' laptop screens

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Web data can contain errors, bias, and protected content, which models may reproduce.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Running more slowly than systems trained…: Speed is unrelated to data source.
• Being unable to answer any question written…: Web data often includes many languages.
• Requiring more electricity to display…: Display power use is unrelated.

Key takeaway: Web-trained models can inherit errors, bias, and IP issues.

stem: A company can improve its recommendation model by collecting more detailed personal data from users. Which approach best balances value and responsibility?

choices.text: Collect only data needed for clear benefit, with user consent and transparency about its use
Collect personal data without telling users, since disclosure might reduce sign-ups
Never use any personal data at all, even with consent, for any recommendation purpose
Collect as much personal data as possible, since more data always makes recommendation models better

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data minimization, consent, and transparency balance model improvement with users' privacy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Collect personal data without telling users,…: Hidden collection breaches trust and often the law.
• Never use any personal data at all, even…: Consented, minimal data can be used responsibly.
• Collect as much personal data as possible,…: More data raises privacy risk without guaranteed benefit.

Key takeaway: Minimize data, obtain consent, and be transparent.

stem: Which TWO practices help a company show that its AI governance is effective, not just documented? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A longer governance policy document with more detailed legal language
A company-wide email announcing that governance is now in place
Periodic internal audits that test whether controls are actually followed
A larger governance committee with more members from each department
Metrics on incidents, reviews completed, and issues resolved over time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Audits and operational metrics provide evidence that governance works in practice.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A longer governance policy document with…: Longer documents do not prove effectiveness.
• A company-wide email announcing that…: Announcements are not evidence.
• A larger governance committee with more…: Committee size does not prove effectiveness.

Key takeaway: Prove governance effectiveness with audits and metrics.

stem: Which TWO controls best reduce the risk of employees over-trusting AI outputs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Present AI outputs as final decisions that employees cannot question
Hide the AI system's known error rates from the employees who use it
Remove any mention that outputs were generated by AI from the interface
Show confidence indicators or sources alongside AI outputs
Train employees on the system's limitations and when to verify outputs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Visible sources or confidence cues and training on limitations help people calibrate trust and verify when needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Present AI outputs as final decisions that…: Unquestionable outputs remove human judgment.
• Hide the AI system's known error rates from…: Hiding error rates prevents calibrated trust.
• Remove any mention that outputs were…: Hiding AI involvement increases over-trust.

Key takeaway: Help users calibrate trust with sources, confidence, and training.

stem: A company uses AI to summarize customer complaints for executives. Which risk to fairness should be checked?

choices.text: Whether the summaries are delivered on Monday morning or on Friday afternoon
Whether complaints from some customer groups are systematically underrepresented in summaries
Whether executives read the summaries on their phones or on their laptops
Whether the summaries use the company's preferred font and color scheme

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Summaries can systematically omit certain voices, such as complaints written in different languages or styles, which skews executive attention.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Whether the summaries are delivered on…: Delivery timing is irrelevant to fairness.
• Whether executives read the summaries on…: Reading device is irrelevant.
• Whether the summaries use the company's…: Formatting is cosmetic.

Key takeaway: Check whether AI summaries represent all groups fairly.

stem: A company is creating an AI incident response process after a chatbot gave harmful advice. What is the main purpose of this process?

choices.text: To detect, contain, investigate, and learn from AI failures or harms quickly
To celebrate AI project launches with a company-wide internal communications plan
To negotiate AI vendor contracts before each renewal date arrives
To schedule regular upgrades of the office computers used by AI teams

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An incident process prepares the company to respond to AI failures or harms and improve afterward.

Why the other options are wrong:
• To celebrate AI project launches with a…: Launch communications are not incident response.
• To negotiate AI vendor contracts before each…: Contract negotiation is procurement.
• To schedule regular upgrades of the office…: Hardware upgrades are IT operations.

Key takeaway: Prepare an incident process for AI failures and harms.

stem: A chatbot vendor updates its model without notice, and the company's chatbot starts answering differently. Which practice would have caught this sooner?

choices.text: Automated regression tests on key questions that run regularly against the live system
Waiting for customers to complain on social media before investigating any behavior changes
Asking employees to guess whether the chatbot seems different from last month
Reading the vendor's annual report once a year to learn about product updates

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scheduled tests on representative questions detect behavior changes quickly, whatever their cause.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Waiting for customers to complain on social…: Customer complaints come after harm.
• Asking employees to guess whether the…: Guessing is unreliable.
• Reading the vendor's annual report once a…: Annual reports are too infrequent.

Key takeaway: Monitor AI behavior with regular regression tests.

stem: A company's AI model is highly accurate but uses a feature that is a close proxy for a protected characteristic. What should governance require?

choices.text: Add more proxy features so that no single feature has a large effect on the predictions
Assess whether using the feature causes unfair outcomes, and remove or mitigate it if it does
Keep the feature, since high accuracy justifies any feature the model happens to find useful for prediction
Hide the feature's name in documentation so that reviewers do not ask questions about it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Proxies for protected characteristics can produce discriminatory outcomes; they must be assessed and mitigated even if they improve accuracy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Add more proxy features so that no single…: More proxies can worsen the problem.
• Keep the feature, since high accuracy…: Accuracy does not justify discrimination.
• Hide the feature's name in documentation so…: Hiding features undermines accountability.

Key takeaway: Assess and mitigate proxies for protected characteristics.

stem: A company rates itself 'advanced' in AI maturity because it has run 30 pilots. None are in production. How should this be assessed?

choices.text: Maturity cannot be assessed until the company runs at least one hundred pilots
Maturity is advanced, since the number of pilots run is the main indicator of an organization's AI maturity
Maturity is closer to early stage, since operating AI in production with measurable value is missing
Maturity is irrelevant, since only the number of AI tools purchased matters

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Maturity reflects the ability to deliver and sustain value in production, not the count of experiments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Maturity cannot be assessed until the…: A pilot threshold is not a maturity measure.
• Maturity is advanced, since the number of…: Pilot counts measure activity, not maturity.
• Maturity is irrelevant, since only the…: Tool purchases are not maturity.

Key takeaway: AI maturity is shown by value delivered in production.

stem: A readiness review finds the company has good data but no process to decide which AI projects get funded. Which gap is this?

choices.text: A data quality gap that prevents models from producing accurate predictions
A talent gap that prevents the company from hiring enough data scientists
An infrastructure gap that prevents the company from running its models reliably at scale
A governance and portfolio management gap that prevents prioritized investment

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lacking a funding and prioritization process is a governance and portfolio management gap, not a data or infrastructure issue.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A data quality gap that prevents models from…: Data is described as good.
• A talent gap that prevents the company from…: Hiring was not the finding.
• An infrastructure gap that prevents the…: Infrastructure was not the finding.

Key takeaway: Missing prioritization processes are a governance gap.

stem: A company's AI models need data that currently takes three weeks to extract from legacy systems. What foundational improvement helps most?

choices.text: Asking data scientists to type the legacy data manually into shared spreadsheets each week
Automated, reliable data pipelines that deliver the needed data on a regular schedule
Waiting for the legacy systems to be retired before starting any AI work at all
Buying more laptops for the data science team so they can extract data faster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automated pipelines make data available reliably and quickly, which AI use cases need to run and be refreshed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Asking data scientists to type the legacy…: Manual entry is slow and error-prone.
• Waiting for the legacy systems to be retired…: Waiting for retirement delays value indefinitely.
• Buying more laptops for the data science…: Laptops do not fix extraction delays.

Key takeaway: Automated data pipelines are a core AI foundation.

stem: A company plans generative AI across departments and wants consistent security and cost control. Which foundation fits best?

choices.text: A single shared password for all employees to access every model the company has approved
Separate accounts with each team choosing any model provider it likes and managing its own security settings
A shared, governed access layer to approved models with central logging, guardrails, and cost tracking
No central controls, so that each team can move as fast as possible without any coordination

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A central, governed access layer gives consistent guardrails, logging, and cost visibility while teams build use cases.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A single shared password for all employees…: Shared passwords are insecure and unaccountable.
• Separate accounts with each team choosing…: Fragmented choices produce inconsistent security and costs.
• No central controls, so that each team can…: No controls create risk and cost surprises.

Key takeaway: Provide a governed, shared access layer for generative AI.

stem: Employees ask whether AI will change how their performance is evaluated. Which leadership response builds trust?

choices.text: Announce that performance will be measured only by how often each person uses the AI tools
Avoid the question until the rollout is fully complete, so that employees stay focused on their current work
Tell employees that nothing will ever change, even though roles are expected to change
Explain openly how roles and evaluation will change, and involve employees in defining new expectations

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transparent communication and involvement in defining expectations reduce anxiety and build trust.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Announce that performance will be measured…: Usage counts are a poor performance measure.
• Avoid the question until the rollout is…: Avoidance breeds uncertainty.
• Tell employees that nothing will ever…: False reassurance damages trust later.

Key takeaway: Be transparent about how AI changes roles and evaluation.

stem: A company wants to build a culture of responsible experimentation with AI. Which practice supports this best?

choices.text: Encourage small, safe experiments with clear guardrails and share lessons from both successes and failures
Punish teams whose AI experiments fail, so that only guaranteed successes are ever attempted by the company
Allow unlimited experimentation with production customer data and no review of any kind
Restrict experimentation to a single executive who decides what everyone else may try

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Safe experimentation with guardrails and open sharing of lessons builds learning without undue risk.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Punish teams whose AI experiments fail, so…: Punishing failure stifles learning.
• Allow unlimited experimentation with…: Unrestricted use of production data is risky.
• Restrict experimentation to a single…: Centralizing all experiments limits learning.

Key takeaway: Encourage safe experiments and share lessons openly.

stem: Which leadership behavior most accelerates AI adoption across a company?

choices.text: Leaders delegating all AI discussion to IT and avoiding the topic personally
Leaders announcing AI goals once and not referring to them again afterward
Leaders asking teams to adopt AI while exempting themselves from using it
Leaders visibly using AI tools themselves and sharing how they apply them

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Visible leadership use signals commitment and shows practical value, encouraging others to follow.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Leaders delegating all AI discussion to IT…: Delegating entirely signals low priority.
• Leaders announcing AI goals once and not…: One-time announcements fade.
• Leaders asking teams to adopt AI while…: Exempting themselves undermines credibility.

Key takeaway: Leaders accelerate adoption by using AI visibly.

stem: A company has scaled an AI tool, and requests for new features are piling up from every department. Which approach manages this best?

choices.text: Build every requested feature immediately so that no department ever feels ignored by the product team
A product-style backlog prioritized by value, with a clear owner making trade-off decisions
Let the loudest department decide which features are built each quarter
Stop accepting feature requests so the team can focus on maintenance only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Treating the AI tool as a product with a prioritized backlog and an owner keeps development focused on the highest value.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Build every requested feature immediately so…: Building everything is unsustainable.
• Let the loudest department decide which…: Volume of complaints is not a prioritization method.
• Stop accepting feature requests so the team…: Refusing all requests stops improvement.

Key takeaway: Manage scaled AI tools as products with prioritized backlogs.

stem: A multinational wants to roll out an AI assistant in countries with different languages and regulations. Which approach reduces risk?

choices.text: Adapt and validate the assistant for each market's language and rules before launching there
Let each country build its own assistant from scratch without sharing any components
Launch the same configuration everywhere at once, since AI works exactly the same way in every country
Launch only in the headquarters country and forbid other offices from ever using it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Market-by-market adaptation and validation address language quality and regulatory differences while reusing the core solution.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Let each country build its own assistant…: Rebuilding everywhere wastes effort.
• Launch the same configuration everywhere at…: One configuration may fail language or legal requirements.
• Launch only in the headquarters country and…: Forbidding other offices forgoes value.

Key takeaway: Localize and validate AI for each market before launch.

stem: After scaling an AI tool, usage drops in several teams after three months. What should leaders do first?

choices.text: Replace the tool with the newest product available on the market immediately
Mandate daily usage for every employee and monitor compliance each week
Talk to users to understand why usage fell and fix the causes they identify
Assume the tool is no longer needed and shut it down across the company

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Understanding the reasons for declining use, such as poor fit, quality, or workflow friction, allows targeted fixes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replace the tool with the newest product…: Switching tools without diagnosis may repeat the problem.
• Mandate daily usage for every employee and…: Mandates do not address root causes.
• Assume the tool is no longer needed and shut…: Shutting down may waste value.

Key takeaway: Diagnose adoption drops with users before acting.

stem: Which TWO questions assess whether a company's culture is ready for AI? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Has the company chosen a mascot for its AI transformation program yet?
Does the company use the latest version of its office productivity software?
Does every employee have a personal parking space at the headquarters office?
Are teams comfortable experimenting and learning from failed attempts?
Do leaders make decisions using data and evidence rather than instinct alone?

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A culture of experimentation and evidence-based decision-making is a strong predictor of successful AI adoption.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Has the company chosen a mascot for its AI…: Mascots are cosmetic.
• Does the company use the latest version of…: Software versions are technical, not cultural.
• Does every employee have a personal parking…: Parking is unrelated.

Key takeaway: AI-ready cultures experiment and decide with evidence.

stem: Which TWO data foundations most enable a company to scale AI use cases? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A catalog that makes trusted datasets easy to find and understand
Keeping all data on individual laptops for faster local access by analysts
Manual data exports emailed between teams on request
Separate copies of the same dataset maintained by every team
Consistent data quality checks built into the pipelines

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Discoverable, trusted, quality-checked data lets teams build new use cases quickly and safely.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keeping all data on individual laptops for…: Laptop storage prevents sharing and is insecure.
• Manual data exports emailed between teams on…: Manual exports are slow and uncontrolled.
• Separate copies of the same dataset…: Separate copies create inconsistency.

Key takeaway: Catalogs and built-in quality checks make data AI-ready at scale.

stem: A company's AI program is led entirely by IT, and business units see it as 'IT's project.' Which change best improves ownership?

choices.text: Stop reporting AI results to business units so they are not distracted
Rename the program so it sounds less technical to business leaders
Make business leaders co-own AI initiatives and accountable for their outcomes
Give IT sole control of all AI decisions to avoid any confusion about ownership

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Business co-ownership ties AI to business outcomes and drives adoption; IT provides platforms and expertise.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stop reporting AI results to business units…: Hiding results reduces engagement.
• Rename the program so it sounds less…: Renaming does not create ownership.
• Give IT sole control of all AI decisions to…: Sole IT control reinforces the problem.

Key takeaway: Business leaders must co-own AI outcomes.

stem: Which TWO practices help sustain AI value after enterprise rollout? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Removing the feedback channel so users focus on using the tool as delivered
Ongoing measurement of outcomes against targets with regular reviews
Disbanding the project team immediately once the rollout is announced
Stopping all monitoring once the system has run for one month successfully
A funded team responsible for maintenance, updates, and user support

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sustained value requires continued measurement and a team to maintain and improve the system.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Removing the feedback channel so users focus…: Feedback drives improvement.
• Disbanding the project team immediately once…: Disbanding leaves no one to maintain it.
• Stopping all monitoring once the system has…: Problems can appear long after launch.

Key takeaway: Sustain AI value with ongoing measurement and a funded support team.

stem: A company debates whether to wait for perfect data before starting AI or to start with imperfect data. Which approach is most practical?

choices.text: Buy third-party data to replace all internal data, regardless of relevance or cost
Start where data is good enough for the use case, and improve data quality as value is proven
Wait until all company data is perfectly clean before starting any AI use case at all
Ignore data quality entirely, since modern AI models fix any data problems automatically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data is rarely perfect. Starting where it is good enough and improving it alongside proven value balances progress and quality.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Buy third-party data to replace all internal…: External data may be irrelevant and costly.
• Wait until all company data is perfectly…: Perfect data may never arrive.
• Ignore data quality entirely, since modern…: Models do not automatically fix poor data.

Key takeaway: Start with good-enough data and improve it as value is proven.

stem: A company's model predicts equipment failures but only after the failure has begun. Operations want earlier warnings. What change to the model's design is needed?

choices.text: Reduce the amount of sensor data used so the model runs faster on each reading
Change the color of the alert messages so operators notice them more quickly
Increase the number of employees who read the model's alerts after each failure has already begun
Train it to predict failures a set time ahead, using data from before past failures started

explanation:
Why this is correct:
To give earlier warnings, the model must be trained to predict a future window, using signals from before past failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reduce the amount of sensor data used so the…: Less data does not create earlier predictions.
• Change the color of the alert messages so…: Alert color does not change timing.
• Increase the number of employees who read…: More readers do not change when alerts occur.

Key takeaway: Define the prediction target to match when the business needs to act.

stem: A museum wants visitors to ask spoken questions about exhibits and hear spoken answers. Which combination of capabilities fits?

choices.text: Fraud detection, document extraction, and translation of exhibit labels into codes
Image generation, sentiment analysis, and demand forecasting for exhibit visitor numbers
Speech-to-text, a question-answering model grounded in exhibit information, and text-to-speech
Recommendation systems alone, since they can hear and answer spoken questions directly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spoken Q&A needs speech recognition, a grounded answering model, and speech synthesis.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fraud detection, document extraction, and…: These do not address the need.
• Image generation, sentiment analysis, and…: None of these handle spoken Q&A.
• Recommendation systems alone, since they can…: Recommendation systems do not process speech.

Key takeaway: Voice assistants chain speech-to-text, answering, and text-to-speech.

stem: A company wants a model to follow its brand voice across thousands of product descriptions. Prompts alone give inconsistent results. What is the logical next step?

choices.text: Fine-tune a model on examples of approved brand-voice descriptions
Switch to a speech model that reads descriptions aloud in a brand voice
Remove the brand guidelines from the prompt to simplify the request
Increase the temperature so the model explores more varied styles

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When prompting cannot achieve consistent style, fine-tuning on approved examples teaches the model the desired voice.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Switch to a speech model that reads…: Speech models do not write text descriptions.
• Remove the brand guidelines from the prompt…: Removing guidance worsens results.
• Increase the temperature so the model…: More variety reduces consistency.

Key takeaway: Fine-tune when prompting cannot reach consistent style.

stem: An assistant must answer questions using both a product database and policy documents. Which design fits best?

choices.text: Let the assistant query the database for facts and retrieve policy passages, then combine both in its answer
Use only the database and ignore the policy documents to keep the design simple
Ask the model to recall database values and policies from its general training data
Put the entire product database and all of the policy documents into every single prompt for completeness

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Structured facts come best from database queries, and unstructured policies from retrieval; combining both grounds answers in each source.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use only the database and ignore the policy…: Ignoring policies leaves questions unanswered.
• Ask the model to recall database values and…: The model does not know internal data.
• Put the entire product database and all of…: Sending everything is impractical and costly.

Key takeaway: Combine database queries and document retrieval for grounded answers.

stem: Which TWO factors most affect whether a model trained last year still performs well today? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Whether the company changed its office furniture during the past year
Whether employees renamed the folder where the model's reports are saved
Whether the patterns in the real-world data have changed since training
Whether the company's website uses a new color scheme for its homepage
Whether the population the model serves has shifted in important ways

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Changes in data patterns and in the population served (drift) are the main reasons model performance declines over time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Whether the company changed its office…: Furniture is irrelevant.
• Whether employees renamed the folder where…: Folder names are irrelevant.
• Whether the company's website uses a new…: Website colors are irrelevant to model performance.

Key takeaway: Data and population drift degrade models over time.

stem: A company wants to reduce customer wait times. Option 1 is an AI chatbot; option 2 is fixing a confusing checkout page that causes most support calls. Which reasoning is sound?

choices.text: Do both at the same time without assessing which one addresses the underlying cause
Fix the root cause first, since removing the source of calls may deliver more value than automating answers
Always choose the AI chatbot, since AI solutions are more modern and impressive than fixing existing web pages
Do neither, since customer wait times cannot be improved by technology changes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AI is not always the best answer; removing the root cause of demand can be simpler and more valuable than automating responses to it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Do both at the same time without assessing…: Acting without analysis wastes effort.
• Always choose the AI chatbot, since AI…: Modernity is not a reason.
• Do neither, since customer wait times cannot…: Both options can improve wait times.

Key takeaway: Consider non-AI fixes to root causes before automating symptoms.

stem: A company sets an AI vision of 'augmenting every employee.' Which step makes this vision actionable?

choices.text: Buy an AI license for every employee in the company and consider the vision achieved immediately
Repeat the vision statement in every company meeting without further planning
Wait for employees to find their own uses without any guidance or measurement
Identify priority roles and tasks where AI assistance creates the most value, with targets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Translating the vision into prioritized roles, tasks, and targets turns aspiration into a plan.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Buy an AI license for every employee in the…: Licenses alone do not create value.
• Repeat the vision statement in every company…: Repetition without plans does not deliver.
• Wait for employees to find their own uses…: Unguided adoption is uneven.

Key takeaway: Turn AI visions into prioritized, measurable plans.

stem: A company introduced AI to answer HR questions. Which measure best reflects employee experience value?

choices.text: The length of each answer produced by the assistant in words
Time to resolve HR questions and employee satisfaction with the answers
The number of times the assistant's name was mentioned in emails
The number of HR policies stored in the AI assistant's knowledge base

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Faster resolution and satisfaction show whether employees are better served.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The length of each answer produced by the…: Length is not experience quality.
• The number of times the assistant's name was…: Mentions are not value.
• The number of HR policies stored in the AI…: Policy counts are inputs.

Key takeaway: Measure employee experience by resolution time and satisfaction.

stem: A company worries a competitor will copy its AI-powered feature within months. Which strategy best sustains its lead?

choices.text: Keep improving the feature with proprietary data and customer feedback faster than competitors can
Hide the feature from customers so competitors do not learn it exists
Lower prices on all products across the catalog to discourage competitors from building the same feature
Patent the idea of using AI for the feature and stop investing in improvements

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Continuous improvement fueled by unique data and feedback keeps a lead even when the initial idea is copied.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hide the feature from customers so…: Hiding the feature forfeits its value.
• Lower prices on all products across the…: Price cuts do not protect the feature's advantage.
• Patent the idea of using AI for the feature…: Stopping investment invites catch-up.

Key takeaway: Sustain AI advantage through continuous, data-driven improvement.

stem: Which TWO practices improve the credibility of AI value reporting to executives? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Change the success metrics each quarter to match whatever improved
Replace measured results with projections whenever results disappoint
Report only the best-performing week of results each quarter
Report results against the baseline and targets agreed before launch
Include costs and negative side effects, not only benefits

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Consistent baselines and targets, plus full costs and side effects, make reports trustworthy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Change the success metrics each quarter to…: Shifting metrics prevents honest evaluation.
• Replace measured results with projections…: Substituting projections hides reality.
• Report only the best-performing week of…: Cherry-picking undermines credibility.

Key takeaway: Credible AI reporting uses fixed baselines and includes costs.

stem: A company wants to use AI to enter a new market segment. Which TWO factors most determine whether AI creates a real advantage there? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The number of AI press releases the company has published
The number of AI conferences its executives attend each year
Ability to integrate AI into the segment's customer workflows
The size of the company's headquarters building
Access to data about that segment that competitors lack

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Proprietary segment data and workflow integration create value customers experience and competitors cannot quickly replicate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The number of AI press releases the company…: Press releases do not create advantage.
• The number of AI conferences its executives…: Conference attendance is irrelevant.
• The size of the company's headquarters building: Building size is irrelevant.

Key takeaway: AI advantage in new markets needs unique data and workflow integration.

stem: A company can invest in one large AI transformation program or in a sequence of smaller initiatives. It has limited AI experience. Which approach is usually wiser?

choices.text: One large program immediately, since big investments always produce bigger returns
A sequence of smaller initiatives that build capability and evidence before larger bets
Invest in whichever option the lowest-cost vendor happens to recommend during its sales process
No investment until AI technology stops changing, to avoid choosing the wrong tools

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With limited experience, staged initiatives reduce risk, build skills, and create evidence to justify larger investments later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One large program immediately, since big…: Large programs carry higher risk for inexperienced organizations.
• Invest in whichever option the lowest-cost…: Vendor recommendations are not a strategy.
• No investment until AI technology stops…: Waiting forgoes learning.

Key takeaway: Build capability through staged initiatives before large AI bets.
